title: State Pension uprating analysis 2026
figure_text: "-£15 billion" in "2039 to 2040" (Table 1: "In-year AME savings (nominal terms, rounded to nearest billion, negative values denote savings)"); "-£11 billion" in "real terms, 2025 to 2026 prices" (Table 2)
comparison: The adjusted Triple Lock vs the triple lock: State Pension spending in 2039-40, nominal, Great Britain; direct effects on AME only, no tax or debt interest
note: DWP estimates annual nominal Great Britain direct AME savings using Pensim3, rounded to £1bn, excluding tax and debt-interest effects; it applies a path for uprating that it does not publish. Ours is the gross saving in Great Britain in 2039-40 on the OBR's central path: one scenario, not an expected value, since the binding C2 score withdrew that. The two do not allow a like-for-like comparison; see HL3774 (answered 15 October 2026), https://questions-statements.parliament.uk/written-questions/detail/2026-10-05/hl3774.

title: Budget 2026
figure_text: "Adjusting the Triple Lock is estimated to reduce State Pension spending by £15 billion a year by the late 2030s, and by £50 billion a year by the late 2040s" (paragraph 1.29, chapter 1; its footnote 61 cites DWP, "State Pension Uprating", October 2026)
comparison: The adjusted Triple Lock vs the triple lock: State Pension spending by the late 2030s, the government's own figure, from DWP's analysis
note: The Budget takes its figures from DWP's uprating analysis: Great Britain, nominal, direct AME, for 2039-40 and 2049-50. Ours is the gross saving in Great Britain in 2039-40 on the OBR's central path, one scenario. The £50 billion falls after our horizon, which ends in 2039-40, so nothing here compares with it. Neither the OBR's October 2026 forecast (its policy table 1.1) nor the Treasury's policy costings and Table 6.1 itemise a costing of the adjustment.

title: Economic and fiscal outlook - October 2026
figure_text: "in our current medium-term forecast an uprating of 2.5 per cent would apply under both the previous and adjusted version of the triple lock in both 2030-31 and 2031-32" (paragraph 3.50, footnote 17)
comparison: The State Pension's rise in April 2030 (2030-31) under the adjusted Triple Lock, on the OBR's October 2026 medium-term forecast
note: The OBR has incorporated the adjusted Triple Lock into its forecast from 2030-31, where it changes no State Pension cost because both rules pay 2.5% in 2030-31 and 2031-32. Ours is the rise the central path pays under the adjusted Triple Lock in April 2030; its statutory inputs to 2030 are the same forecast's quarterly CPI and earnings.

title: Long-term economic determinants, March 2026 EFO
figure_text: "Average earnings growth plus 0.6 percentage points" (the note on the 'Triple lock' growth rate, sheet "Growth rate assumptions", column "Notes on 2025 Long-term economic determinants")
comparison: The OBR's long-term growth-rate assumption for triple-lock uprating, above average earnings growth (points a year)
note: The OBR's premium is an assumption for its long-term projections; in the sheet's 2026 column the 'Triple lock' rate is 0.56 points above average earnings growth (4.31% against 3.75% a year). Ours is the expected triple-lock rise less May-July earnings growth for the April 2034-2039 rises (inputs of 2033-2038) under the primary distribution: rule arithmetic, not a fiscal figure.

title: Economic and fiscal outlook - October 2026
figure_text: "Averaging over the period as a whole, state pension payments would have been on average 1.4 per cent lower each year than under the current triple lock and 4.4 per cent higher than under earnings uprating" (paragraph 3.51, Chart 3.4: outturn earnings and inflation, 1990 to 2025, pension values from 1990)
comparison: The adjusted Triple Lock against the triple lock, replayed on outturn earnings and prices
note: The OBR averages payments over 35 years of outturn from a 1990 start. Ours is the adjusted Triple Lock's flat rate over the triple lock's after the April 2026 rise, replayed on the published September CPI and May-July earnings (April 2022's earnings leg suspended, as in law) with the adjusted rule starting in April 2017: one decade, read at its end rather than averaged. The OBR adds (paragraph 3.52) that the adjustment would reduce the projected long-term rise in debt by around 25% of GDP in 2075-76, beyond any horizon here.

title: Fiscal risks and sustainability - July 2025
figure_text: "we estimate that uprating by the triple lock rather than earnings will have added £15.5 billion (0.5 per cent of GDP) to state pension spending annually by 2029-30. This is around three times higher than the £5.2 billion we estimate the triple lock would have cost by that point under initial assumptions"
comparison: Triple lock vs earnings uprating since its introduction in April 2012: extra State Pension spending in 2029-30; the £5.2bn is that cost on the assumptions of the original 2010 costing and its long-run expectation of rises 0.2 points a year above earnings
note: OBR compares the triple lock with earnings uprating since 2012, in 2029-30. Ours is the gross saving in 2026-27 had the adjusted Triple Lock, which keeps the higher of CPI and 2.5% as a floor, started in April 2012.

title: What a ratchet! (Curtice and Clegg)
figure_text: "The OBR estimates spending on the State Pension would have been £12.6 billion lower this year with earnings-linked uprating than it is set to be with triple lock uprating, which we estimate would be a net saving of around £9 billion when we take account of lower income tax receipts and higher means-tested benefit spending."
comparison: Triple lock vs earnings-linked uprating, State Pension spending "this year" (2026-27 when RF wrote): £12.6bn gross is the OBR's estimate, £9bn net of income tax and means-tested benefits is RF's
note: RF's summary describes the same £12.6bn as against "a smoothed earnings link since 2012"; the report's own text attributes it to the OBR, against earnings-linked uprating. Ours is the net saving in 2026-27 had the adjusted Triple Lock (which keeps a CPI and 2.5% floor) started in April 2012.

title: Fiscal risks and sustainability - July 2026
figure_text: State pension spending, "which is projected to rise from 5 per cent of GDP to around 9 per cent of GDP over the projection period in the baseline. This is driven by population ageing and the cost of triple-lock uprating (calculated based on historical inflation and earnings volatility). In a scenario where the state pension is instead uprated in line with average earnings, state pension spending reaches around 7 per cent of GDP."
comparison: Triple lock vs earnings uprating over the 50-year projection to 2075-76, with the triple lock's cost calibrated to historical inflation and earnings volatility, % of GDP
note: A 50-year horizon in % of GDP with ageing; ours is in £bn for 2039-40 with survey ages held fixed, on the OBR-wedge scenario: the central path with the triple lock paying the 'Triple lock' row of the OBR's March 2026 long-term determinants (average earnings growth plus 0.6 points beyond 2030-31), the OBR's own allowance for how often CPI or the floor beats earnings. One scenario, not an expected value.
